This is a within-node tension, because easy verbal access to the trauma is hard to square with marked fragmentation and severe re-experiencing-linked formulation here.

vignette: John is a 57-year-old North American male who has been seeking help for symptoms that have progressively worsened since he experienced a sexual assault about six months ago. John is single and works as a tutor, an occupation where his interactions with others can often be challenging. The traumatic event occurred in the evening when John was walking home from work. A man suddenly grabbed him and forced him into a nearby alley, severely violating him both physically and emotionally. The clarity of this memory remains vivid for John; every detail is etched deeply in his mind, but he also feels like parts are missing and that he can't fully articulate what happened. Since the assault, John has been hyper-vigilant, constantly watching others around him for signs of potential danger. This constant monitoring has made it difficult for him to engage normally with people, leading to a growing sense of isolation and feeling set apart from others. He finds himself avoiding any situation where he might feel strong emotions or be touched by another person. John's triggers are deeply rooted in the traumatic event: physical touch, being forced into something against his will, and the presence of men can all bring back intense feelings of fear and distress. These triggers not only remind him of the assault but also fuel his sense of constant threat and vulnerability. For example, during a tutoring session with a male student, John would become so anxious that he would leave early or cancel future appointments. This hyper-vigilance and avoidance have led to a deterioration in both his professional and personal life. He avoids unfamiliar places because the fear of not being able to assess danger is overwhelming. Even choosing where to sit becomes an exercise in safety assessment, whether it's at a restaurant or during a community meeting. The vividness of his memories also contributes significantly to John's struggles. Whenever he is triggered, those clear and detailed recollections come flooding back, making him feel as though the assault is happening all over again. He knows what happened but finds it impossible to find words to describe these experiences, which further isolates him from others. John has developed a number of maladaptive strategies to cope with his symptoms. One such strategy is smoking, which provides a temporary escape from the anxiety and fear he feels. Avoiding emotional stressors by steering clear of situations where he might feel strong emotions or physical touch helps him manage the immediate distress but further isolates him. The cycle begins to tighten when John's negative appraisals exacerbate his symptoms. He believes that his body is no longer reliable, making it difficult for him to trust even simple bodily sensations. This lack of trust extends to everything around him, contributing to a constant state of vigilance and avoidance behaviors. The fear of not being able to control the situation has made him avoidant in social settings and overly cautious, often leading to isolating behaviors that reinforce his negative beliefs. John's current state is one of profound distress. He recognizes that he can no longer function effectively at work or maintain any meaningful relationships due to these overwhelming fears and memories. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his quality of life had drastically declined, and he desperately wanted to regain a sense of normalcy and trust in himself and others. In therapy sessions, John hopes to learn how to manage his triggers more effectively and find ways to reconnect with people without feeling constantly on guard. He is seeking support to break this cycle and restore some level of safety and control over his life.
